Claude Startups pauses the free Team year and the $1,000 API credit offer after demand blew past expectations.

Claude@claudeai
Replying in a thread
We’ve loved seeing so many founders join the Claude Startups program. Unfortunately, we underestimated demand for the program, and we need to pause the Claude Team and $1,000 API credit offers.

With hundreds of thousands of applicants, we're re-reviewing applications so the program can serve as many startups as possible.

If you’ve already claimed the Claude offers, they’ll still remain in your account.

If you applied or were approved and haven’t claimed the offer, we're re-reviewing your application. Unfortunately, this means that some accounts who had already been approved will not get access to the offer. We know this is disappointing and we’re very sorry.

All accepted program members still have access to the Startup Stack and Applied AI office hours. If you're on a Claude Max or Team plan, your monthly API credits are available in Console as usual.

We appreciate your patience, and we're working to get you building as quickly as we can.
Sarah Wolf@sarahzorah· Oct 8
We didn’t anticipate the demand for the Claude Startups program. In the first 48 hours of the program, we received 21x the number of applications compared to the last 5 months it’s been live.

We let way too many people in this time, so we’ll need to pause on giving out the Team plan and API credits benefits. The other benefits (Startup Stack, Applied AI office hours/events) will remain. If you’ve already claimed the Claude offers, they’ll still remain in your account.

We didn’t properly tune the acceptance criteria at the start, and many non-startups were accepted this time around. We’re fixing this now. We’re sending an email now to everybody who hasn’t claimed their benefits yet, and will re-verify those applications so we can keep Claude Startups for startups 🙏

6 days and $40K of compute with GPT-5.6 Sol found a full-chain Chrome exploit (XBOW's $250K bounty). Argues these tools help defenders.

Greg Brockman@gdb
6 days and $40,000 of compute with GPT-5.6 Sol to find a critical vulnerability in Chrome, claiming Google’s first full-chain reward in 2026 for a vulnerability that would affect an estimated 1 billion users.

Highlights the opportunity for defenders to utilize these tools to secure their software to unprecedented levels:
Oege de Moor@oegerikus· Oct 13
For the second time in Google Chrome’s history, Google awarded a $250,000 bounty for a full-chain exploit… to @XBOW. Here’s the full story:

At an all-hands at the start of 2026 in Malta, I set the team a crazy challenge. A full-chain exploit of Chrome by the annual Black Hat cybersecurity conference in August.

I believed there were few better tests of whether @XBOW could move beyond web applications to desktop software, servers and devices.

Chrome is one of the most hardened pieces of software on the planet, used by more than half the world’s population.

A full-chain exploit lets an attacker take total control of a machine, where they can read every email, password and bank login the user types. You don’t need to download anything or click a phishing link. Visiting the wrong site is enough.

So @moyix, Andres Luksenberg, Baul Lee, and Willem Pinckaers took on the challenge along with a fifth teammate: OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol.

They built a chain they thought would win, but Google told us they already knew one of the bugs.

We were already in Las Vegas for Black Hat and DEF CON, and the team didn’t want to go home without the win.

So Brendan and the agents built a new exploit in just 6 days.

We submitted it to Google and waited.

The news came through that we'd done what should’ve been impossible. A full-chain bounty of $250,000, the first awarded under Google’s 2026 rules.

It took just 6 days and $40,000 of compute to construct an exploit that affects a billion users of Chrome on Windows. An intelligence-agency veteran told me his team used to spend 6 months on this kind of vulnerability.

My takeaway: the cost of finding truly critical vulnerabilities is collapsing, for attackers and defenders alike. Restricting powerful models is not the answer; GPT-5.6 Sol is already public.

But defenders have one advantage attackers never will: they can test their own code first.

Assume your software is exploitable. Whoever is hunting your bugs has the same building blocks we did.

This is cause for urgency but not panic.

XBOW is now developing an autonomous product for testing compiled software (desktop applications, servers, embedded devices), and partnering with the world’s top organizations to design that product.

If you’d like to be one of them, get in touch.

P.S. Restart Chrome whenever the Update button appears!

Not featured above, so here it is in full.

Boris Cherny@bcherny
I am surprised that people are surprised this is how I prompt Claude.

Talk to Claude the way you would a coworker. There's no secret to prompting. There's no need to be overly scaffolded or prescriptive for most tasks -- give Claude a goal, and it will figure it out.

Back in the Sonnet 3.5 days, your prompt mattered a lot. Nowadays, it's much more important to communicate to the model:

1. What you want it to do
2. How much effort you want it to spend
3. How it should verify that it did the right thing
